crime.value: Murder by gunshot, with the body planted in an innocent man's car trunk plus forged love letters and a faked photograph to frame him; central question: who put her there and why does the evidence point to Frank?
crime.quote: There was a bullet hole in her forehead.

victim.value: Cora Miller, attractive brunette in her early thirties, wife of Encinal county auditor Thurman Miller; killable because she refused to divorce her husband, who wanted to marry a young blonde
victim.quote: He's got him some young blonde on the string. He wants to marry her. Cora won't give him a divorce.

closed_world.value: The small-town orbit of Kingsbury and nearby Encinal, narrowed to the brief window when Frank's car sat unattended behind Pop Lassiter's beer joint during his farewell chess game
closed_world.quote: The only time anyone could have tampered with my trunk was while I had my car parked back of Pop's place.

culprit_and_motive.value: Thurman Miller shot his wife so he could marry his blonde mistress after Cora refused a divorce; Pop Lassiter, an ex-con forger, was paid to design the frame-up (forged letters, photo, duplicate trunk key)
culprit_and_motive.quote: He shot Cora tonight, and brought her over here... Then he put her in the trunk of your car, usin' that key I'd had made

resolution.value: Deputy Buddy notices the rim of Pop's barroom clock left in the enlarged snapshot, traces the camera angle to a side room in Pop's bar, confronts Pop (who has a forgery conviction); Pop confesses to the frame-up and names Thurman, who is arrested and gives a full statement
resolution.quote: whoever did the enlargement left the rim of that clock, up there, on one corner of the print.

investigator.value: Dual lens: Frank Judson, the framed newspaperman narrating as prime suspect investigating his own frame-up, aided by Buddy, his friend and deputy sheriff who actually solves it
investigator.quote: Buddy was a good friend... But he was also a deputy sheriff.

suspect_architecture.value: Narrow cast: Frank Judson (framed narrator, apparent suspect with letters/photo as manufactured motive), Pop Lassiter (ex-con bar owner with forgery record, opportunity via trunk key), Thurman Miller (husband, motive: blonde mistress and refused divorce, actual killer), Buddy the deputy sheriff (friend/investigator, briefly suspected of nothing). Differentiation is by criminal record, access to the car, and marital motive.
suspect_architecture.quote: Pop Lassiter himself was the most logical suspect. He was a mean old devil, and an ex-con, and capable of anything.

red_herring.value: The forged love letters in Frank's handwriting, the snapshot of him inscribed 'I love you, Cora Darling', and the body planted in his trunk — an entire fabricated affair designed to point at Frank; secondarily Pop Lassiter's criminal past misdirects toward him as the murderer rather than the accomplice.
red_herring.quote: The writer, who had the same name and handwriting as myself had committed himself on paper to being hopelessly in love with Cora Miller.

clue_fairness.value: Fair: the reader sees the photograph described (close-up, indoors, grainy, possibly enlarged from a negative) and Pop's list of prior convictions before Buddy interprets them; the clock rim in the print is the crop detail that is shown to the reader as Buddy examines it.
clue_fairness.quote: "Looks like it was taken indoors by available light." He bent closer, squinting his eyes. "Pretty grainy. Could be blown up from part of a negative."

social_world.value: Small-town Texas/Gulf-coast world of Kingsbury and Encinal: a respectable county auditor, a newspaperman drifter, a deputy sheriff friend, and a disreputable ex-con bar owner. Everyone knows everyone; gossip in Pop's beer joint is the information network, and the transient outsider is the easiest man to frame.
social_world.quote: "Cora Miller comes from this town. She's one of Ed Shelby's girls. I've known the Shelbys all my life."

alibi.value: Frank has no alibi — the body rode with him unstopped from Kingsbury. Pop's implicit alibi is being at his closed bar; Thurman's cover is domestic normalcy plus 'recognizing' Frank on sight, which Buddy notes proves nothing.
alibi.quote: I had not stopped once, even for gasoline, since I left there two hours ago.

reveal_mechanic.value: Photographic reconstruction: Buddy spots the rim of Pop's wall clock left in the cropped enlargement, back-calculates the camera angle to the dark side room in Pop's bar, demonstrates it on site, and confronts Pop with his forgery conviction — producing a confession naming Thurman Miller.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "whoever did the enlargement left the rim of that clock, up there, on one corner of the print. I recognized it as the one on Pop's wall."

media_and_audience.value: Lightly present: Frank is a newspaperman, and the framers count on how the evidence would 'read' publicly — letters 'the kind that would cause a judge to clear the courtroom' — i.e. a scandal narrative packaged for a jury.
media_and_audience.quote: the kind that would cause a judge to clear the courtroom before it was read aloud to the jury

investigator_wound.value: Frank's rootlessness: a drifter with no ties, quitting jobs and towns, which is exactly what made him a usable patsy; the case forces him to confront that a rolling stone gathers no friends, ending with him staying, reclaiming his job and Emily.
investigator_wound.quote: not only does a rolling stone gather no moss, it also does not gather friends. You have to stay in one place to do that.

victims_enemies.value: Cora Miller's husband Thurman, the Encinal county auditor, wanted to marry a young blonde mistress and Cora refused him a divorce; he shopped for a killer among local ex-cons, approaching Pop Lassiter with a cash offer months in advance.
victims_enemies.quote: He's got him some young blonde on the string. He wants to marry her. Cora won't give him a divorce.

suspect_wounds.value: Frank Judson is a rootless drifter who loudly broadcast his discontent and departure plans in a bar — his transience, quit job, and New Orleans reservation make him look exactly like a fleeing lover. Pop Lassiter's ex-con record (manslaughter, marijuana, forgery) makes him look guilty of more than he did.
suspect_wounds.quote: I've seen 'em like him all my life. Drifters. Transients.

unreliable_frame.value: First-person narration by the frame-up victim, whose own handwriting, signature and photograph testify against him — the documentary record contradicts his memory, so the reader must weigh his protest against forged 'evidence' of a two-month affair he denies.
unreliable_frame.quote: The writer, who had the same name and handwriting as myself had committed himself on paper to being hopelessly in love with Cora Miller.

setting_as_constraint.value: Small-town Texas geography (Kingsbury/Encinal, thirty miles apart) plus a night thunderstorm and a detour blowout: the culprit relied on Frank's unbroken drive to New Orleans, and only one window existed — the car parked in the dark behind Pop's beer joint during the customary farewell chess game.
setting_as_constraint.quote: He was parked back of my place in the dark, waiting for you to drive up and play that last chess game with Buddy.

evidence_type.value: Photographic/physical: the cropped enlargement of Frank's snapshot retained the rim of a distinctive wall clock, letting Buddy triangulate the camera position to a dark side room in Pop's bar.
evidence_type.quote: whoever did the enlargement left the rim of that clock, up there, on one corner of the print.

false_suspect.value: Frank Judson himself — the framed narrator, arrested by his deputy friend; secondarily Pop Lassiter, whom Frank violently accuses of the murder though he only forged the letters and photos.
false_suspect.quote: Frank, I have to tell you this. You're under arrest now, and anything you say can be held against you.

technical_detail.value: Available-light photography with fast film and special processing (no flash, hence grainy negative enlarged and cropped), plus handwriting forgery and a duplicate car-trunk key made in advance.
technical_detail.quote: No flash was used. There's enough light here for fast film, and the right kind of processing.

moral_ambiguity.value: Pop Lassiter draws a line he thinks is moral — refusing to kill for money while selling the scheme that made the killing possible — and Thurman kills not from malice but from a trapped marriage he could not legally exit.
moral_ambiguity.quote: I'm not going to get myself in that kind of big trouble. But I told him I could figure a way he could do it
